feedback: If structures are mislabelled: cross-check against where the nucleus, cytoplasm and membrane sit relative to the cell outline.
If the drawing is shaded or unlabelled: a biological drawing uses clear lines and labels, not shading, so the recording meets the 'record' standard.
activities.intendedInsight: Working with a genuine specimen is the real goal: the cells you see are actual structures in actual tissue, reinforcing that living material is built from cells.
learnerActions: Where lab access allows, prepare a wet-mount slide of onion epidermis and/or stained cheek cells.
Start on the lowest-power objective, focus using coarse then fine adjustment, and use only fine focus at higher power while observing the real specimen.
Identify nucleus, cytoplasm and cell membrane in the live view (in onion cells the visible outline is mainly the cell wall; the membrane is pressed against it and usually not distinguishable).
Produce a labelled biological drawing of the cells you observe.
activities.title: Real bench microscope slide work

feedback: For a wrong artefact choice: recall that bubbles have a thick dark edge and a bright, empty centre with no cytoplasm or nucleus, while cells have a boundary enclosing cytoplasm and often a nucleus.
For a mismatched label: re-locate the dark (stained) nucleus — often, but not always, near the centre — and the surrounding cytoplasm within the cell boundary.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recognition of named structures and reliable discrimination of real cells from artefacts.
learnerActions: Match each structure to its name (nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane).
Choose which of several images is an air-bubble artefact rather than a cell.
Trace the outline of the cell membrane around an animal cell (e.g. a cheek cell) in a micrograph.
activities.title: Consolidation checks: structure, name and artefact

feedback: If the pupil still pictures cells as flat: rotate the model to show depth and relate the top-down view back to the micrograph.
activities.intendedInsight: Cells are not flat, empty boxes; the flat image is one slice through a three-dimensional structure.
learnerActions: Explore a rotatable 3D onion or cheek cell and relate it to the flat micrograph.
Describe how the microscope view is a thin optical section of a three-dimensional object.
activities.title: Enrichment: the micrograph is a slice of a 3D cell
